problem: Standard VLMs encode the image once, feed-forward, so the vision encoder cannot attend to task-specific small cues (e.g. subtle human social behaviour) that the LLM could identify. Existing visual reasoning relies on text CoT or external tools (boxes, segmentation) that break gradient flow.
motivation: Robots in human-shared spaces must interpret dynamic, subtle human behaviour and intentions, which needs finer visual cues than the default encoding gives. The LLM knows what to look for, so feeding its understanding back to the vision encoder could let the model re-look at the scene.
key_idea: A lightweight gated-MLP module projects the LLM's last-layer hidden states for image tokens back into the vision encoder's input (added to the image embedding) for a second forward pass, forming a language-to-vision reasoning loop.
insight: Reinterpreting rather than replacing the image works: removing the original image in pass two lowers Mementos (2.318 to 1.950) and navigation results. Naive image duplication baselines degrade, so gains are not from extra visual tokens. The MLP matters for navigation and Mementos, but 'No MLP' matched intention accuracy (37.50 vs 36.97), likely because the learned patch unmerger compensates. Gains are largest for weaker base models (Gemma/LLaVA on intentions), and navigation gains are limited by output formatting or refusals.
method: Visual reasoning loop: take LLM final-layer hidden states at image-token positions after pass 1, project through the module and add to the image embedding before the vision encoder.
Gated MLP: sigma(W_g x) ⊙ W_p(Dropout(W_2 GELU(W_1 x))), hidden dim 2x the LLM hidden dim.
Patch unmerger: learned layer mapping LLM-space tokens back to the number of patches the encoder expects.

Two-pass training: pass 1 (LoRA optionally enabled) yields the hint; pass 2 (LoRA disabled) feeds prompt, original image and the new image; loss only from pass 2, LLM and encoder frozen, gradient flows through the encoder to the reasoner.
Training data and recipe: Visual-CoT, images at 360p, 7-LR sweep, top-2 configs (chosen on MME-CoT) merged by linear interpolation; <1.7% params trainable (<3% with LoRA).
Inference: same two passes, so ~3x TFLOPs (7.06 to 20.39) and throughput falls 4.24 to 1.27 samples/s.
New human-intention dataset: 376 four-option MCQ samples from 188 annotated events in a Furhat HRI study with 10 participants.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma 3 4B, LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 4B (frozen LLM and encoder; trained reasoner module, optional LoRA)
setting.training_data: Visual-CoT (general image-question-reasoning data), images resized to 360p; no robotics data
setting.observation: monocular RGB frames (single egocentric image per step)

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark such as R2R is used; navigation is reported only as average final distance to goal. The benchmark splits are not specified (labels are approximate).
results: On Qwen 7B the module reduces navigation distance (7.787 to 7.530), raises the Mementos score (2.261 to 2.318) and intent accuracy (34.04% to 36.97%). Gemma 4B and LLaVA 4B gain strongly on intention accuracy (20.84% to 31.65%; 20.74% to 25.53%) and modestly on Mementos, but navigation gets slightly worse. Cost is about 3x compute.
limitations: Navigation gains are small and inconsistent (worse for Gemma and LLaVA due to JSON formatting failures and refusals); navigation is evaluated only by final distance to goal.
About 3x inference FLOPs and 3.3x lower throughput from the double pass.
Evaluation is small and non-standard: a self-collected intention dataset of 10 participants, absolute accuracy stays low, and there are no significance tests or real-robot experiments.
